passages.title: Allah's threefold favour upon the Prophet
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Inshirāḥ 1–4: Allah's threefold favour upon His Messenger ﷺ

**What this passage is about.** In four short ayat Allah reminds His Messenger ﷺ of three gifts already given to him: his chest was opened wide, the burden that was weighing down his back was removed, and his name was raised high. What holds them together is not only that they are all favours, but that they are all put as a *question* — "Have We not…?" — and that every one of them is done, in the Arabic, *for him*.

## The setting: a surah of favours

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that from Sūrah aḍ-Ḍuḥā to the end of the Qurʼān, twenty-two surahs are mainly concerned with the divine favours conferred upon the Prophet ﷺ and with his greatness; only a few are concerned with the conditions of the Hereafter or some other subject. Sūrah al-Inshirāḥ belongs squarely to that group — it is concerned with the *special* favours Allah conferred upon him.

And it continues the previous surah even in its manner of speech. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the style is the same interrogative style: aḍ-Ḍuḥā asked, "Did He not find you…?"; here it is, "Did We not cause your bosom to be wide open for your benefit?" (ayah 1). A question like this is not asking for information. It is the gentlest possible way of making someone *notice* something they already know. Allah is not informing the Prophet ﷺ that his chest was opened; He is inviting him to remember it — and to reason from it.

## Ayah 1 — the opening of the chest

The verb is *sharḥ*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the word literally denotes "to open, to cause the bosom to be widely opened." Not to fill, not to strengthen — to *widen*. Something that was narrow is made spacious.

Ibn Kathir glosses it: "have We not opened your chest for you" — meaning, "We illuminated it, and We made it spacious, vast and wide." Two things at once, then: light and room.

He anchors this in another verse where the same verb appears:

> "And whomsoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his breast to Islam." (6:125)

That parallel is worth sitting with. The opening of the chest is what Allah does for the one He wills to guide — the same act, named with the same verb, is what the Prophet ﷺ is being reminded of here.

**What was it opened *for*?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says: in this context, to cause the bosom to be wide open to comprehend the divine mysteries. Allah illuminated his bosom with wisdom, divine light and peace, and made it spacious, vast and wide. His bosom was expanded to receive the knowledge and wisdom and the gracious morals and ethical qualities which — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it — the greatest philosophers could not match.

And then a consequence Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out: as a result of this expansion of heart, *tawajjuh ilal-makhlūq* — attentiveness to the creation — did not disturb his attentiveness to and concentration on Allah. That is what "spacious" amounts to here: turning to people did not cost him his turning to his Lord.

**Did the angels physically open his chest?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that some of the authentic Traditions report that the angels, with Allah's permission, physically opened the blessed chest of the Prophet ﷺ, and that some of the commentators interpret this "expansion of the chest" in ayah 1 as referring to that same miracle — noting that this is mentioned in Ibn Kathir and others. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān itself does not settle the question, closing with "And Allah knows best!" So this is best held as the commentators held it: the verse is explained as the illumination and widening of his heart, and some commentators additionally read it as pointing to the physical opening. Both are transmitted; neither should be pushed as the single meaning.

**One more thing Ibn Kathir draws out.** He adds that just as Allah expanded his chest, He also made His Law vast, wide, accommodating and easy, containing no difficulty, hardship or burden. The inward gift is mirrored in the outward religion. A spacious heart was given a spacious sharīʿah — and what was given to the Prophet ﷺ personally spills over onto everyone who follows him.

## Ayat 2–3 — the burden lifted off his back

> "And removed from you your burden. Which weighed down your back?"

**The words.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *wizr* as, literally, "burden," and the phrase *naqḍ uz-ẓahr* as "to break one's back — as, for instance, when a heavy load is put on one's back, it bends." The verse signifies that Allah had relieved him of his burden that was breaking his back. Ibn Kathir notes of the verb in ayah 3 simply that *al-Inqāḍ* means *the sound*; he does not elaborate further. And Ibn Kathir reports that more than one of the Salaf said of "which weighed down your back": it means "its burden weighed heavy upon you."

**What was the burden?** Here the commentators genuinely differ, and the sources present more than one answer rather than one settled view.

*Ibn Kathir's reading* is that "And removed from you your burden" means what Allah says elsewhere:

> "That Allah may forgive you your sins of the past and the future." (48:2)

*Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two answers.* The first: now and then the Prophet ﷺ did certain permissible deeds, thinking that they were of benefit and in the interest of spiritual development; later on he discovered that they were not in keeping with wisdom, or were undesirable. He was conscious of his high status and close proximity to Allah, and he regarded even such things as serious infractions. That, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, was naturally a very heavy load that made him grieved — until Allah relieved him of it, in that a blanket pardon was granted to him and it was declared that he would not be held accountable for such things.

Notice what this view is actually describing. On Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own terms these were *permissible* deeds — the weight came from the sensitivity of a heart standing that close to Allah, where the merely unwise registers as a grave failing. And Allah's response, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it, was not correction but pardon: the weight taken off entirely.

The second answer Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from some commentators: *wizr* refers to the effect of revelation, which weighed heavily on him in the initial stages of prophethood. He was saddled with a nerve-racking and back-breaking task — raising a morally degenerated people through the propagation of tawḥīd and the elimination of kufr and shirk, and then through them cleansing and purifying the whole of mankind of iniquity, ignorance and superstition. The task enjoined was:

> "So, stand firm — as you have been commanded." (11:112)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the Prophet ﷺ used to feel the heavy weight of this task and responsibility; some narrations report that a few strands of his beard had turned grey as a result of this command, and he ﷺ is reported to have said that this verse — "So, stand firm as you have been commanded" — had made him old. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this without naming a collection, so it is passed on here exactly as it stands, with no attribution beyond that.)

Hold that beside ayah 3 and the picture is complete: a man feeling the weight of that task and responsibility, greying under the command to stand firm — and Allah saying, *We removed it from you.*

**How was it removed?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the halves of the passage together. Ayat 2–3, it says, give the cheerful news that Allah will remove from him the load which was weighing down his back; the verses that follow show *how* the back-breaking load will be removed, and that every difficulty will be followed by ease and relief. And it adds this: by means of the expansion of the bosom, Allah gave the Prophet ﷺ so much courage that no instance of hardship seemed a hardship, and no burden of any magnitude seemed a burden.

That is a profound way of reading the sequence. On this reading the relief did not only come from outside; the heart was enlarged until the load no longer weighed as a load. Ayah 1 turns out to be the answer to ayah 3.

## Ayah 4 — "and We raised high for you your name"

> "And have We not raised high your fame?"

Notice the tense. It is not a promise for later; it is a completed act: *We raised it.*

**Mujahid** said of this ayah: "I (Allah) am not remembered except that you are remembered with Me: *I bear witness that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.*"

**Qatadah** said: "Allah raised his fame in this life and in the Hereafter. There is no one who gives a sermon, declares the Testimony of Faith (Shahādah), or prays a prayer (Ṣalāh) except that he proclaims it: *I bear witness that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.*"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same in its own words: the meaning of raising the name of the Prophet ﷺ is that his blessed name is remembered together with the name of Allah in all the symbols of Islam — the kalimah, the adhān, the iqāmah, and in sermons from the minarets and pulpits throughout the world. And it adds an observation anyone can test: no sensible person utters the Prophet's ﷺ name without respect and honour, even though he may not be a Muslim.

Take these together and the fulfilment of ayah 4 is not a fact you have to go and look up in a history book. It is in the words a Muslim says to enter the religion, in the call to prayer, in the iqāmah, in the sermon.

One thing is worth reading carefully in the wording of the testimony itself, as the sources quote it. The two halves are not parallel claims. The first is about worship: there is no god worthy of worship except Allah. The second is about office: Muhammad is the *Messenger* of Allah. His name is joined to Allah's name in the remembrance — not shared with Him in worship. That distinction is written into the very sentence in which his name was raised.

## The hidden grammar: it was all *for you*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note under the heading "Note Carefully," and it is the key that locks these ayat together as one unit.

Three verses, three favours bestowed on the Prophet ﷺ: (1) opening of the bosom widely, (2) removal of the burden, (3) raising of the name high. And each of the sentences, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out, is composed the same way — a verb, an object, and *between them a prepositional phrase*:

- *sharḥ ṣadr* — "…**for your benefit**…" (ayah 1)
- *waḍʿ wizr* — "…**from you** your burden" (ayah 2)
- *rafʿ dhikr* — "…**for you** your name" (ayah 4)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's conclusion is that this indicates the essential characteristic and special greatness of the Prophet ﷺ, in that all of this is done for the sake of him. The little phrase sitting inside each sentence is not filler; it is the point.

## Living it

**Read your own life the way this passage reads his.** Ayat 1–4 are put as a question, and the honest answer to a question like this is always *yes*. Before anything else, Allah walks His Messenger ﷺ back through what has already been given. That is a discipline worth borrowing when the present feels unbearable: count what is already in your hands before you count what is missing.

**Ask for the wider chest, not only the lighter load.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point is that the load was removed by way of the expansion of the bosom — courage given until no hardship seemed a hardship. And in 6:125, cited by both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, opening the breast is precisely what Allah does for the one He wills to guide. It is His to give, and it is worth asking Him for.

**Take the ease of the Law seriously.** Ibn Kathir's remark — that Allah made His Law vast, wide, accommodating and easy, containing no difficulty, hardship or burden — is not decoration. If your practice of the religion feels like a back bending under a load, that may be a sign to look again at how you are carrying it, rather than at what Allah revealed.

**Say his name knowing what you are saying.** The kalimah, the adhān, the iqāmah, the sermon — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names these as the very places where ayah 4 is fulfilled. When you say those words, you are standing inside the answer to Allah's question. Let that turn a reflex into an act of love.

passages.title: With hardship comes ease, so strive
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is saying

These four ayat are the hinge of the sūrah. After Allah has reminded His Messenger ﷺ of what He has already done for him — opening his breast, removing the burden that weighed down his back, raising his fame high (ayat 1–4, all quoted by Ibn Kathir at the head of his commentary) — the sūrah moves on. Ayat 5 and 6 give the promise: along with hardship there is ease. Ayat 7 and 8 give the response: not idleness while waiting, but exertion — when you have finished, devote yourself to Allah's worship, and turn to your Lord with eagerness.

So the unit moves in one arc: **past favours → the promise → the work that follows.** Certainty about Allah's help is not meant to leave a believer passive; the very next word after the promise is a command to exert himself.

---

## "Along with hardship there is ease" — and again

Ibn Kathir's comment on ayat 5–6 is brief and weighty. Under the heading "Ease after Difficulty" he writes: "Allah informs that with difficulty there is ease, and then reaffirms this information (by repeating it)." So on his reading the second ayah is not an ornament — it is a reaffirmation of the first, the same news given again so that it lands.

Notice, too, how the commentaries render the words. Ibn Kathir: "Verily, along with every hardship is relief." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: "So undoubtedly, along with hardship there is ease." Not ease at some distant point beyond the difficulty, but ease *along with* it — the wording keeps the two close together.

---

## The grammar that opens the passage up: one hardship, two eases

This is where Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does its most valuable work, and it turns on a single feature of Arabic that is easy for an English reader to miss.

In Arabic, the definite article *al-* works roughly like "the" in English: it points to something already known. Maʿārif states the principle plainly: if a noun carries *al-* and is repeated with *al-*, both instances "refer to the same antecedent" — that is, to the same thing. But if the same noun is repeated **without** the article, the two occurrences "refer to different antecedents."

Now look at the two ayat:

- **Ayah 5:** *fa-inna maʿa **al-**ʿusri yusrā* — "So, surely with **the** hardship comes *an* ease."
- **Ayah 6:** *inna maʿa **al-**ʿusri yusrā* — "Surely with **the** hardship comes *an* ease."

*Al-ʿusr* — "the hardship" — carries the article in both. So, Maʿārif says, the second is "the repetition of" the first: "It does not refer to a new hardship." But *yusr* — "ease" — occurs in both ayat **without** the article. So the ease of ayah 6 is a different ease from the ease of ayah 5.

Maʿārif draws the conclusion: **there is only one hardship and two eases.** And it immediately guards against a flat, arithmetical reading: "'Twofold ease' does not mean twice as much. In fact, it means 'manifold ease'." As Maʿārif puts it, "only one kind of hardship will face him, but in the wake of it many kinds of ease are assured."

This is a case where the meaning genuinely lives in the Arabic. Read in translation, ayah 6 can look like a simple echo of ayah 5. Read as Maʿārif reads it, the second ayah adds a whole further consignment of relief.

---

## The morning the Prophet ﷺ came out in a happy mood

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān preserves a report from Sayyidnā Hasan al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) that puts flesh on the grammar. He relates that the Prophet ﷺ once emerged from his home in a very happy mood and, giving cheerful news to his Companions on the basis of this very ayah, said: **"One hardship cannot overcome twofold ease."**

Picture the setting. These were people under real pressure — the hardship was not theoretical. And the Messenger ﷺ comes out to them visibly cheerful, carrying not a strategy but this sentence, and hands it to them as good news. That is what a promise from Allah is meant to do to a believer's face.

Maʿārif draws a second grammatical observation out of this narration. The *al-* in *al-ʿusr* is here what grammarians call *al- lil-ʿahd* — the article "used to indicate previous knowledge," pointing to something the listener already has in mind. Maʿārif says it "refers to the hardship of the Holy Prophet ﷺ and his Companions." This was not an abstract maxim floated into the air; it was a promise about the hardship they were actually living through. And Maʿārif notes that Allah kept it in plain sight: "history and biographical books written by Muslims and non-Muslims — all bear ample testimony to fact that the most difficult task, even the seemingly impossible task, became easy for him."

---

## "But my hardship has not lifted"

Maʿārif anticipates the honest objection, and its answer protects the reader from two errors at once.

"If a person does not achieve 'ease' after 'hardship', it does not contradict this verse." The ayah is not a mechanical guarantee that every believer's difficulty resolves on a schedule he can see. "In fact," Maʿārif continues, "even now Allah's universal principle applies."

What is asked of the one still waiting, Maʿārif lists concretely:

- **exercise fortitude** against the hardship;
- **rely on Allah with purity of heart** — *tawakkul*, reliance placed on Allah, and undivided;
- **devote yourself totally to Him**;
- **hold onto high hopes for His grace**;
- **do not despair of His mercy if there is delay in success.**

And the assurance that closes it: "He certainly will grant relief after every instance of hardship." Maʿārif attributes this discussion to *Fawāʾid-e-ʿUsmāniah* and adds that hadith narratives support it.

Note what is *not* promised here — a timetable — and what *is*: that relief comes, and that delay in success is not evidence against it. Despair, not difficulty, is what the passage forbids.

---

## Ayah 7: "So when you have finished, exert yourself"

Having settled the heart, the sūrah puts the body to work. *Fa-idhā faraghta fanṣab.*

**The key word.** Maʿārif notes that *fanṣab* derives from *naṣab*, which means **"to be tired."** So the verse "signifies that one should tire oneself when carrying out acts of worship." And Maʿārif draws the practical edge: "One should not carry out acts of worship only when one finds it convenient." Even binding yourself to a *wazīfah* — Maʿārif's own gloss is "a usual course of optional worships," a fixed regular practice you hold yourself to — "is itself quite exerting and tiring, no matter how little."

**What "finished" means.** Ibn Kathir explains ayat 7–8 as: "when you have completed your worldly affairs and its tasks, and you have broken away from its routine, then get up to perform the worship, and stand for it with zeal, complete devotion and purify your intention and desire for your Lord." Mujahid said of this ayah: "When you are free from the worldly affairs, and you have stood to pray, then stand up for your Lord."

**A note on scholarly difference.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here. Its reading — that the Prophet ﷺ is commanded, when he has finished his day's work of teaching and training his followers and other temporal affairs, to turn to Allah with all his heart — is "the interpretation assigned to this verse by most commentators." Maʿārif adds: "Some scholars have interpreted it differently, but the foregoing interpretation appears to be the closest." The reader should know that the ayah has been read in more than one way, and that what follows is the position of the majority as Maʿārif reports it, not a point beyond discussion.

---

## Direct worship and indirect worship

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the ayah out into a principle it addresses specifically to teachers and preachers — its own heading is "The Command for Teachers and Preachers to Remember Allah During Spare Hours" — and the distinction it draws is worth sitting with.

The Prophet ﷺ "exerted himself greatly to spread the word of Allah and reform human beings." That labour, Maʿārif says, "was his greatest form of 'worship' but it was 'indirect worship' through planning and executing the plan of human reform." And then the point of the ayah: "the indirect worship is not sufficient." When he is free from collective services to humanity, he should devote time to **direct worship** — Maʿārif names it as prayers, remembrance of Allah, supplication and seeking Allah's pardon, including prayer for the success of his efforts — "because this 'direct worship' is what man is created for."

Then comes the observation that explains the very wording of the ayah. Why does Allah speak of *finishing*, of being free? Because, Maʿārif suggests, the indirect worship is the kind you *can* finish: "that is based on need, and a believer can free himself from it, but the 'direct worship' of Allah is such that he cannot free himself from it. He has to spend his entire life and expend all his energy in it." The one duty you are never off duty from is your Lord.

Maʿārif attaches a warning for scholars involved in education, propagation and human reform: they "should not be unmindful of 'direct worship'." Time should be devoted **specifically, in privacy**, to attentiveness to and remembrance of Allah — because, as the biographies of the righteous predecessors testify, without it "neither education nor preaching can be effective. It would be devoid of light and blessings."

---

## From the Sunnah: worship with an undivided heart

Ibn Kathir supports his reading of ayat 7–8 with two prophetic statements, both bearing on the same idea — that one should come to worship free, not with the mind tugged elsewhere.

The first he describes as "a Hadith that is agreed-upon to be authentic": there is no prayer when the food is served, nor when the two foul things — excrement and urine — are pressing a person.

The second, which he introduces simply as a further statement of the Prophet ﷺ: when the prayer has started and the dinner has been served, then begin with dinner.

Read alongside ayah 7, these are not permission to postpone worship for comfort. They are the other side of the same principle: settle the business first — the meal, the need — precisely so that when you do stand before your Lord you stand with a whole heart and nothing pulling at you. Finish, then exert yourself. (Ibn Kathir relays both without naming a collection, so they are given here exactly as he gives them.)

---

## Ayah 8: where the longing goes

*Wa ilā rabbika farghab.* Ibn Kathir renders it: "And to your Lord turn intentions and hopes" — and his explanation of the two ayat together ends on exactly this note: "purify your intention and desire for your Lord." Maʿārif renders it "towards your Lord turn with eagerness." The translation given with the ayah in our text is "turning to your Lord ˹alone˺ with hope."

So the ayah does not merely say *want*; it says where the wanting must go. Effort in ayah 7, longing in ayah 8: the body exerts itself in worship, and the heart's desire is aimed — at Allah. And it is the same passage that has just delivered the promise of manifold ease which now tells the believer where to send his hope.

---

## Living it

Drawn only from what these commentaries say, the passage asks four things:

1. **Take the promise as news, not merely as comfort.** The Prophet ﷺ received it happily enough to come out to his Companions and tell them. It is information about how Allah deals with His servants: one hardship, and in the wake of it manifold ease.
2. **When success is delayed, do not read the delay as refusal.** Maʿārif is explicit that unrelieved hardship "does not contradict this verse." Hold fortitude, purity of reliance, and high hope of Allah's grace — and refuse to despair of His mercy.
3. **Do not let the promise make you idle.** The command that follows is *fanṣab* — from a root meaning "to be tired." Bind yourself to a regular practice, however small, and keep it when it is inconvenient; Maʿārif says that itself is exerting and tiring, no matter how little it is.
4. **Keep private worship alive underneath public service.** Whatever your work for others — teaching, calling people to Allah (*daʿwah*, the work of propagation and reform), service of any kind — Maʿārif insists it cannot substitute for turning to Allah directly. That is the worship you were created for, and the one you never finish.
